where: the record strip on sync-orphaned, against the same strip on sync-merged, sync-differs, sync-failed and sync-profile
finding: With sync-merged added, the record strip now exists in five states on the glass and four of them share one silhouette: message left, actions held at the right edge, comparison full width beneath. Orphaned is the fifth, and it is a different object — the whole action stack has fallen onto a second row at the container's left edge, so a 1152px-wide strip carries all of its content in the left half and leaves the right half empty for the strip's full height. It is not a styling difference, it is a wrap, and the thing that causes it is a 168-character guarantee sentence sitting inside the action column: at its 320px cap it claims the column's full width, the message column's 384px floor plus that no longer fits the 609px inner measure, and the row breaks. That is exactly the under-40-character rule written down for merged this round, broken by a sibling. It costs the reader the family resemblance in the one state where the strip is most consequential, and it leaves the primary action floating in the middle-left of a void rather than at an edge.
evidence: sync-orphaned: strip 511–1152, inner 528–1136; message 529–999, guarantee caption 528–845 over four lines, 'Re-create her in Planning Center' 528–847, 'Discard the edit' 624–751. The rectangle x 1005–1140 × y 172–492 has zero deviation from the strip background — 135×320px of untouched fill, and below y 320 the empty band widens to x 848–1140. Compare sync-merged (message 529–930, actions to 1136), sync-differs, sync-failed (546–935 / to 1136) and sync-profile (550–963 / to 1136), all of which reach both edges. Note also that the caption sits above the primary here and below it on sync-merged — the same slot, opposite order.
direction: The guarantee is prose about what happened, not a label on a button; move it into the message column where the rest of the narration already lives, and leave beside the button only the short guard the family's own rule allows. Do it and orphaned collapses back into the four-sibling silhouette with no other change. While the slot is being settled, fix its order too: the guard belongs on one side of the primary across the whole family, not above it in one state and below it in another.

where: the strip paragraph and the Profile card's Planning Center provenance line
finding: The rule this round set for differs — a value or a time that appears in a cell does not appear in the paragraph — is not held by the scene that was built to prove the family. The strip's prose names both people and the day, and then the two-up directly beneath names both people and the day again, so the object built to be read at a glance is a recap of the sentence above it rather than the answer to it. Across the page the survivor's name is set five times and the day four, which is what pushes the paragraph to six lines and what breaks the provenance line: it overruns its measure and splits the one action phrase in the card, leaving a single orphaned word underlined on its own line. The reader is being told the same two facts in four registers and the layout is paying for it in both blocks.
evidence: sync-merged: 'Ava Chen-Ito' appears in the h1 (y 90), the strip button (y 195), the strip paragraph in bold (y 213), the left cell (y 375) and the provenance line (y 1011); 'Tue/Tuesday' appears in the identity chip, the paragraph, the right cell's '#AC101 · merged Tue' and 'since Tuesday's merge'. The paragraph runs six lines to y 313 where differs' runs six to the same depth on strictly less content. Provenance line: line one runs 528–1100 against a card inner edge of 1136, and 'profile' wraps alone to 528–579; on sync-failed the same line ends at 864 whole and unbroken.
direction: Apply the family's own rule to its newest member. Let the paragraph carry only what the cells cannot — that a merge happened and that the correction followed it and changed nothing — and let the two ids, the two names and the day live once each in the cells built for them. The provenance line can then say where the record is read from without restating the merge date, and the action phrase will sit whole on one line as it does on the other four record scenes.

where: the middot between the strip's bold heading and its body, on sync-differs and sync-merged
finding: The strip runs heading and body as one inline paragraph with a middot between them, which composes well when the body actually starts on the heading's line. On the two scenes whose heading fills the measure it does not: the separator is the last mark on line one, set in the body's grey rather than the heading's red, hanging half a space off the end of a bold red phrase with nothing after it. It reads as a stray speck at the rag, or worse as a truncation mark, and it is the only piece of punctuation on these pages that separates nothing. It is small and it is the kind of small that undoes an impression of care the rest of the type has earned.
evidence: sync-differs: 'Planning Center holds a different last name' ends at x 926 and the grey ' ·' trails it, with 'Your correction went out at 9:12…' beginning at x 553 on the next line. sync-merged: identical, heading ending x 932. On sync-failed, sync-profile and sync-orphaned the separator sits mid-line with the body running on after it, which is what the pattern was for.
direction: The separator should only be on the glass when it is doing its job. Bind it to the first words of the body so it can never trail a rag, or let the pair fall back to a stacked heading and body when the heading fills the measure — the same treatment the phone width already uses. Either way no line should end on it.
